mcq.q: Time complexity measures:
o: The amount of time a program with a particular algorithm needs, expressed as a function of input size
The number of lines of code
mcq.e: It does not measure actual seconds.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a reason to study time complexity?
o: To prefer the faster algorithm among several
To reduce the compiled instruction size
mcq.e: Instruction size is part of space complexity.

mcq.q: In T(n) = c + T_A(n), what does c represent?
o: Constant time that does not depend on the input size
mcq.e: c is the insensitive part; T_A(n) is the sensitive part.

mcq.q: Which is the main factor on which time complexity depends?
mcq.e: Input size is the main factor.

mcq.q: The two approaches to determine time complexity are:
mcq.e: Operation count and step count.

mcq.q: In the operation count approach we:
o: Count how many times the key operation(s) are performed
Run the program and time it
mcq.e: Only the operation(s) that contribute most to time are counted.

mcq.q: A weakness of the operation count approach is:
o: Choosing the key operation may be difficult and it does not measure actual execution time
It cannot be used for loops
mcq.e: Success depends on identifying the operations that contribute most.

mcq.q: For max(a, n) the key operation a[i] < a[c] is executed how many times?
mcq.e: c runs from 1 to n-1, giving n - 1 comparisons for any data.

mcq.q: For a = {16, 11, 2, 19, 6}, what does max return?
mcq.e: It returns the INDEX of the largest value: 19 is at index 3.

mcq.q: For find(a, n, x), the best case number of comparisons x != a[c] is:
mcq.e: If x is at index 0, one comparison is enough.

mcq.q: For find, the worst case number of comparisons is:
mcq.e: When x is last or not present all n elements are compared.

mcq.q: If x is present and equally likely at every position, the average number of comparisons in find is:

mcq.e: The standard arithmetic series sum.

mcq.q: In the step count approach, how often is a LOOP (c < n) test evaluated if the body runs n times?
mcq.e: True n times plus one final false evaluation.

mcq.q: Step count T(n) of the iterative sum algorithm (s <- 0, c <- 0, loop, s <- s + a[c], c <- c + 1, RETURN s):
T(n) of the iterative sum for n = 3 is:
Step count T(n) of the recursive sum (IF n > 0 / RETURN a[n-1] + sum(a, n-1) / RETURN 0):
Programming instrumentation means:
o: Adding extra code to a program to collect information about its execution
mcq.e: E.g. a global counter g incremented at each step.

mcq.q: In the instrumented iterative sum, how many times is g++ executed for the last evaluation of c < n?
mcq.e: Only once, after the loop, for the final false test; the n true tests are counted inside the loop.

mcq.q: Which pair is correct?
o: Space complexity: S(n) = c + S_A(n); time complexity: T(n) = c + T_A(n)
mcq.e: Both follow the same constant-plus-sensitive form.

written.q: Define time complexity and give three reasons for being interested in it.
written.a: Time complexity is the amount of time a program written with a particular algorithm needs to run to completion. Reasons: some problems require a real-time response; we prefer the program that runs fast when several algorithms solve a problem; we must guarantee users that the program completes without time-out.

written.q: Explain the two approaches to determining time complexity.
written.a: Operation count: identify one or more key operations (those contributing most to time) and count how many times they are performed. Its weaknesses: it does not measure actual execution time and choosing the key operation may be difficult. Step count: estimate T(n) by accounting for the time spent on all program steps, i.e. the number of steps the program takes to complete.

written.q: Using the operation count approach, find T(n) for the max algorithm (loop c from 1 to n-1 with IF a[i] < a[c]).
written.a: Key operation: the comparison a[i] < a[c], which needs memory fetches of i, c, a[i], a[c] and a comparison. The loop variable c takes the values 1 to n−1, so the comparison is executed n − 1 times: T(n) = n − 1 for all inputs.

written.q: Find the step count of the iterative sum algorithm and verify it for n = 3.
written.a: Lines: s ← 0 (1), c ← 0 (1), loop test (n + 1), s ← s + a[c] (n), c ← c + 1 (n), RETURN s (1). T(n) = 3n + 4. For n = 3: 13. Check by trace: tests 0<3, 1<3, 2<3, 3<3 = 4; body lines 3 + 3; plus 3 single lines = 13.

written.q: Find the step count of the recursive sum algorithm.
written.a: IF (n > 0) is evaluated n + 1 times; the recursive RETURN line runs n times; RETURN 0 runs once. T(n) = (n + 1) + n + 1 = 2n + 2.

written.q: What is programming instrumentation? Show how it would count steps in a loop.
written.a: Modifying a program by adding extra code to collect information about its execution. Declare a global counter g = 0 and write g++ beside each step (declarations, each loop test, the loop body statements, the final failing test, the return). At the end g holds the step count, e.g. 3n + 4 for the iterative sum.
